rationale: The trust grantor role with temporary trust and leased tokens elaborates the control plane's specific function within the plane split architecture.
The recommendation that SSO not bypass ongoing authorization logically requires the control plane to be the authoritative trust grantor.
The worst-case assessment of control plane compromise depends on the control plane being the authoritative trust grantor.
The concept of control plane compromise as a distinct worst case requires the architectural separation of planes to be fundamental.
The four-component authorization architecture refines the control plane/data plane split with a detailed decomposition into isolated enforcement and policy components.
The four-component authorization architecture elaborates the NIST PDP/PEP model by specifying the distinct, isolated components that compose it.
Containing agent data strictly to the control plane is a concrete security application of the plane separation principle.
The trust grantor role explains why agent data must be contained—the control plane needs authoritative access to sensitive agent data to make informed trust decisions.
The danger of SSO bypassing the control plane is underscored by the fact that control plane compromise is the worst-case scenario, so the control plane must remain in the authorization loop.
The NIST PDP/PEP model is a formalized operationalization of the control plane/data plane split, with PDP mapping to the control plane and PEP to the data plane.
The three PEP types—user agent, network, and application—refine the PDP/PEP model by specifying where enforcement occurs across the architecture.
The definition of what qualifies as a PEP—identity-centric, dynamic, automated control channel—provides the criteria for distinguishing between the three PEP types.
The refined PEP definition elaborates the PDP/PEP model by specifying that a traditional firewall alone does not satisfy the PDP-controlled enforcement requirement.
The cloud-boundary PEP recommendation is a specific instantiation of the network PEP type, using source IP restrictions as the enabling primitive.
The cloud-boundary PEP configuration is a concrete example of a component meeting all PEP qualification criteria—identity-centric, dynamic policies via automated control channel.
The three PEP types elaborate where enforcement points sit within the control plane/data plane architecture, distinguishing user-agent, network, and application enforcement.
The GC's four deployment models extend NIST's four by adding cloud-routed and microsegmentation models on top of NIST's resource-based and enclave-based models.
The target-initiated access constraint specifies that the cloud-routed deployment model struggles with server-initiated traffic, narrowing which models remain viable under this requirement.
The target-initiated access constraint reveals that some NIST deployment models handle server-initiated traffic naturally while others do not, refining model selection criteria.
Because the five NIST deployment scenarios compound in real enterprises, the four deployment models must cover the full solution space non-exclusively.
Since enterprises combine multiple deployment scenarios, they need multiple NIST deployment models simultaneously rather than picking one.
The PEP at the cloud boundary is the enabling pattern for the cloud-routed deployment model, which is one of the four models covering the ZT solution space.
The three ZTA approaches—identity governance, micro-segmentation, and SDP—map to specific NIST deployment models, with SDP aligning to device agent/gateway and micro-segmentation to enclave gateway.
The phone-home attack pattern demonstrates why preventing lateral movement is the primary ZT goal, as it is the attack phase that follows initial perimeter compromise.
The phone-home pattern demonstrates why perimeter security alone fails and why the control plane/data plane split is necessary for real-time, identity-centric authorization.
The three types of filtering—host, bookended, and intermediary—form defense-in-depth that directly serves the primary ZT goal of preventing lateral movement.
Enclave design as trust classification directly implements lateral movement prevention by grouping resources with similar trust requirements and controlling access between groups.
The three types of filtering forming defense-in-depth are the network-level implementation of the micro-segmentation ZTA approach.
All three ZTA approaches—identity governance, micro-segmentation, and SDP—directly serve the primary goal of preventing lateral movement through different enforcement mechanisms.
The seven pillars taxonomy provides the functional capability domains that the seven RA principles bridge to implementation, forming the DoD's three-layer architecture.
The DoD RA principles as architectural bridge add a layer above the PDP/PEP model, connecting high-level tenets to PDP/PEP-based implementation.
The DoD's seven-pillar capability taxonomy complements the NIST PDP/PEP model by organizing functional capabilities that the policy engine must orchestrate.
Because ZT is a comprehensive strategy rather than a product, implementation inevitably faces organizational challenges beyond purely technical ones.
The 13 best practices being a sequenced implementation guide with organizational steps demonstrates that ZT is a strategy with methodology, not merely a product.
The 13 best practices elaborate on how ZT improves security across dimensions by providing a specific, sequenced implementation path for each dimension.
The network cross-cutting capabilities maturity model details the specific technical challenges—from manual boundary monitoring to enterprise-wide automation—that ZT implementation must overcome.
The CCCS 13 best practices serve as evidence that a pragmatic implementation guide can be built atop existing frameworks, supporting the recommendation to adopt rather than invent frameworks.
Enclave design as trust classification is a direct application of spatial trust assessment—the architecture location determines what trust data is available for enclave grouping decisions.
Spatial trust assessment refines the control plane's function by showing that trust data availability and granularity vary by architectural location—branch, campus, data center, cloud.
The lack of agent format standardization increases exposure risk if agent data is not contained, reinforcing the need to keep it strictly within the control plane.
The absence of agent format standards highlights a gap in the PDP/PEP model—the policy engine lacks a standardized way to consume agent data from diverse sources.
The network cross-cutting capabilities describe how the control plane matures from static, perimeter-focused policies to dynamic, enterprise-wide automated policy enforcement.
The recommendation that SSO should not bypass the control plane for ongoing authorization depends on the architectural separation of planes being the correct foundation.
Placing the PEP at the cloud boundary is a specific architectural pattern for positioning the data plane enforcement point relative to the control plane in cloud deployments.
Because enterprises compound multiple deployment scenarios, ZT implementation faces compounded organizational and technical challenges across heterogeneous environments.
The GC developing its framework aligned with CISA and NIST pillars exemplifies the recommended approach of building on existing frameworks rather than inventing from scratch.

The primary goal of preventing lateral movement motivates the control plane/data plane split, because real-time authorization at every access attempt is the architectural mechanism that stops lateral movement.
Temporary trust and leased tokens directly prevent lateral movement by ensuring that a compromised session cannot be reused to access additional resources.
